436.t: Father's success story, wine, and Tommy Dorsey at the Hotel Sherman
436.s: His father lived to see their success; Sy Oliver and Dorsey loved his father's wine when the band played Chicago.
436.q: He saw us both having some nice things and seeing us do what he had in mind all through. He was a wonderful guy. I remember I took Ziggy Elman’s place, that was the Herd just before he went in the service, and I took his place with Tommy Dorsey’s band, and Sy Oliver was writing for the band. And at…

661.t: Grandfather and James Reese Europe; Juilliard
661.s: Her grandfather played with James Reese Europe and attended Juilliard, which is why her mother wanted to go there.
661.q: And he also went to Juilliard School. So that’s why my mom wanted to go there.

851.t: A typical week, and growing up with a conductor father and flamenco mother
851.s: His parents' musical backgrounds, then his current activities: DJing, producing events, film scoring and a New Orleans studio.
851.q: I was painting my house, a pretty kind of sea green color. All the things I do are related to music. Because first of all my father was a symphony conductor, a wonderful violinist. He could sight read a transposed score on piano, don’t ask.

142.t: His father's instrument business and visiting Havana musicians
142.s: His father sold saxophones, clarinets and music from a small office, where Cachao, Chocolate Armenteros and Mario Bauza came by; his mother was a seamstress.
142.q: He used to be the agent, very small agent in Havana, or the seller of saxophones. Sell many saxophones and clarinets also, and trumpets. He used to sell also accessories and printed music and things like that. So, that’s why I ran into people like Cachao; he used to go in there to buy his things…

86.t: His mother Kitty, no siblings, and staying out of trouble
86.s: He describes his mother's hard work, her fetching him home from Cleveland, and her attending his dances.
86.q: No, no brothers and sisters. So I feel like that I attributed to her that longevity because I was never a problem, no trouble. She never got a call that I was in jail, it was always a pleasant call when she got a call from me. I was never in trouble. One time I got stranded in Cleveland and I…

328.t: His father Clark and mother Laura
328.s: Hampton explains his name and describes his father as teacher, carpenter, painter and musician, and his mother Laura as a selfless pianist and harpist.
328.q: My dad and my mom were wonderful people. That’s the one thing that I – the one impression that’s very, very – they left with me. After I went out into the world, I found that the standard of values and principles and things that they had was something that you don’t find very often. My father was a…

135.t: Father Percy Sr.: Elks clarinetist and master mechanic
135.s: Heath describes his father's weekend clarinet in the Elks band and his thriving truck and car repair business in the late 1920s.
135.q: My father was a clarinet player, a weekend clarinet player with the Elks . . . with the independent, Benevolent Protective Order of Elks, which is a segregated Elks. It’s a black organization.

373.t: His mother, his father as role model, and his grandparents
373.s: Character sketches of his independent mother and civil-rights-minded father, and a brief note on his grandparents.
373.q: My mother had been a very independent woman, growing up in Orthodox Jewish religion. For example, when her father died, she insisted on saying the prayer for the dead and speaking at the shul, the synagogue. That was rarely done. When she was at Filene’s, she became, I think, a head cashier. Then…

953.t: What he got from his mother: kindness and a love of music
953.s: Rollins describes his mother as soulful, gentle and hard-working, and recalls his devotion to her.
953.q: Well, my mother was a very, I would say a very soulful, in that she loved music, she was a, she was a hard-working person. She went to night school as we were kids, as little kids, she was going to night school.

26.t: His parents never heard him play live
26.s: Greer repeats that his family heard him only on radio and records, and his mother was proud.
26.ch: Image, travel and Black, Brown and Beige
26.q: But as I say, we played everywhere. I never played in my hometown, Long Branch, New Jersey. My mother and father never heard me play. My two sisters never heard me play. My little brother heard me once. That's one thing I always felt sorry for, my parents never lived to hear me playing, my sisters…

66.t: Her stepfather Fletcher Burley, gambler and protector
66.s: Fletcher Burley loved her, was generous and feared in Pittsburgh, and took her into gambling joints under a big coat to play. Mayfield again rescued her from stranded tours.
66.q: He was the kind of a man that he loved me so much he would almost put his own kids aside for me, if I needed anything. Well, he was very charitable. Sometimes I'd bring kids in that didn't have shoes and he'd give them money to buy shoes or to buy clothing. Fletcher had a big coat - this is funny -…

77.t: Her sister Josephine and bringing her mother to Chicago
77.s: Josephine died at 17; Hunter brought her mother to Chicago, who never objected to show business and taught her to always be a lady.
77.q: Josephine? Well, Josephine was only 17 years old when she died. She came to Chicago to see my mother. And that was the first time I had seen her since she was a little tiny girl.
